title: DRIVE — Question Bank (Full) v2
description: Motivation, Engagement Risk & Career Clarity | 10-Archetype Classification System
confidentiality: Engagement Risk data is the most sensitive in the suite — never shared with executive's employer in B2B contexts

bands.interpretation: Strong motivation across multiple dimensions; highly engaged and directed
Generally energised; 1-2 motivation dimensions with meaningful gaps
Partial alignment; significant gaps between role and motivational architecture
Substantial misalignment; disengagement risk is material
Motivational breakdown; urgent career review and role redesign required

primary_motivation_type.step1: Compare D1 (Intrinsic) vs D2 (Extrinsic) — difference ≥10 points → Intrinsic-dominant OR Extrinsic-dominant; <10 → Dual-drive
primary_motivation_type.step2: If D3 (Values Alignment) > both D1 and D2 → Purpose-driven; If D5 (Growth Orientation) > both D1 and D2 → Growth-driven; If both D3 and D5 exceed D1 and D2, use whichever is higher
primary_motivation_type.step3: Drifter flag — when no clear dominant motivation source identified

archetypes.name: Achiever
archetypes.risk: Burns out when recognition dries up

archetypes.name: Craftsman
archetypes.pattern: Motivated by excellence of the work

archetypes.name: Champion
archetypes.risk: Loses motivation when team is removed

archetypes.name: Explorer
archetypes.pattern: Driven by new challenges and contexts

archetypes.name: Restless
archetypes.risk: Exits if mandate does not expand

archetypes.name: Golden Handcuffs
archetypes.pattern: Staying for rewards, not the work
archetypes.risk: Explore what would need to change to re-engage

all_questions.text: The work itself — the intellectual challenge, the problem-solving, the craft — is the primary reason I remain in my current role, not the compensation, the organisation, or external recognition.
I am most motivated when I am working on complex, demanding tasks that require my full attention — routine or administrative work drains my energy regardless of the external rewards attached.
If the external rewards were sufficient — compensation, title, recognition — I would remain engaged even in work I find intellectually undemanding or unstimulating.
There are moments in my current role when I become so absorbed in the work that I lose track of time — a state of flow that I find deeply motivating in itself.
I would stay in my current role even if the external conditions deteriorated — the quality of the work itself is sufficient to sustain my motivation.

In APAC cross-border assignments — where the cultural complexity, ambiguity, and relational demands are inherently rich — I find the work itself more motivating than in simpler, more familiar contexts.
Visible recognition of my contributions — from senior stakeholders, from the organisation, or from my professional community — is an important source of motivation for me.
The compensation, title, and status associated with my current role are meaningful motivating factors — not incidental to my engagement.
When I achieve a significant result, I want it acknowledged — being told quietly that I did well is not enough; I want the recognition to match the contribution.
I would be equally motivated in a role that paid significantly less, as long as the work itself was interesting and the mission was meaningful.
My motivation increases measurably when I am in a high-visibility role — where my work and results are seen by senior leadership or the broader organisation.
Career progression — movement to more senior titles, expanded scope, higher compensation — is an active and ongoing motivator for me, not just a background assumption.
My daily work reflects what I believe is genuinely important — ethically, professionally, and in terms of the impact I want to have.
I can clearly articulate why the work I do matters — not just commercially or organisationally, but in terms of what I personally value.
I am being asked to do things in my current role that conflict with what I believe is right — creating a nagging sense of misalignment I cannot easily resolve.
The organisation I work for conducts itself in ways that align with my personal ethical commitments — I am not required to suppress my values to succeed here.
My current role allows me to contribute to something larger than commercial outcomes — to a purpose or mission I personally believe in.
Even when external conditions are difficult — the work is hard, the organisation is under pressure — I feel that what I am doing matters in a way that sustains my commitment.
I believe I am capable of handling whatever challenges arise in my current role — including the ones I have not encountered yet.
When I face a significant challenge at work, my default response is to lean in — to believe I can figure it out rather than to doubt whether I am the right person for it.
I have a growing sense that the demands of my current role may be exceeding my capability — and that concern is affecting my performance and my wellbeing.
My confidence in my own judgment and capability holds under pressure — I do not significantly second-guess myself when the stakes are high or the situation is ambiguous.
I have made a significant career transition — new sector, new geography, new level of seniority — and successfully rebuilt my confidence and effectiveness in the new context.
In APAC cross-border contexts — where the cultural, relational, and operational demands differ significantly from my baseline — I feel genuinely capable, not just technically competent.
I am more energised by assignments that require me to develop new skills than by assignments where I can apply expertise I have already built.
When my current role stops being challenging — when I feel I have largely mastered what it requires — my motivation declines noticeably, even if external conditions are favourable.
I prefer to operate in domains where I have deep established expertise — new challenges that require me to start from scratch are more uncomfortable than energising.
I actively seek feedback and development input — not because it is expected, but because I am genuinely motivated by becoming more capable.
I would take a role with a significantly steeper learning curve over a role where I would be immediately effective, if both were otherwise comparable.
Taking on a new APAC mandate — with its unfamiliar regulatory, cultural, and relational complexity — is the kind of challenge that energises rather than intimidates me.
If I am honest with myself, there are days when I question whether I would remain in my current role if I were not financially or contractually obligated to do so.

The work I am doing now feels structurally misaligned with what I need — not because the organisation is wrong, but because the role, the mandate, or the level of scope no longer fits who I have become.
I have noticed a persistent decline in my discretionary effort — the extra thinking, the proactive initiative, the willingness to go beyond what is asked — over the past 6–12 months.
Even when external conditions are positive — good team, supportive leadership, interesting work — I find it difficult to feel genuinely energised or committed.
If a significant and attractive opportunity presented itself tomorrow — not just financially, but in terms of scope, challenge, or relational context — I would seriously consider leaving.
There is a part of me that has already mentally left this role — I am going through the motions while waiting for something to change or for the right moment to move.
